item.title: The fate of Mercury's ejected mantle
item.description: arXiv:2611.33297v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Mercury's unusually high core mass fraction, inferred from its high bulk density, remains difficult to explain. Mantle stripping by a giant impact provides a plausible origin, but without efficient removal, the ejected debris remains on Mercury-crossing orbits and later gets re-accreted. Here, we show that re-accretion of impact debris onto Mercury is inefficient, making a giant-impact origin plausible. We combine N-body simulations of giant-impact ejecta with a collisional evolution model and consideration of processes acting on small dust. We find that, when the ejecta are dominated by large, several hundred km-sized non-vaporized fragments, the debris disk remains optically thin and the collisional cascade is truncated near the radiation-pressure blowout limit, where micron-sized grains are removed. In contrast, if vaporized, the ejecta recondense into mm to cm-sized droplets and form an optically thick disk, in which radiation pressure cannot efficiently truncate the cascade. The debris can then be ground down to nanometre-sized grains, where collisions become predominantly non-fragmenting and dissipative rather than destructive. Subsequent inelastic collisions damp the eccentricities and inclinations of the nanodust, producing a geometrically thin disk whose lifetime is governed by removal through exposed surface layers, where grains acquire large charge-to-mass ratios through solar UV radiation and are rapidly removed by electromagnetic forces. In either scenario, collisional evolution strongly reduces the re-accretion of debris and alleviates a key difficulty for the giant-impact origin of Mercury's large core. More broadly, highly energetic giant impacts in the inner regions of planetary systems may lead to short-lived populations of nanometre-sized dust.
item.dc:creator: Tuhin Ghosh, Mark Wyatt, Alan P. Jackson, Oliver Shorttle, Maximilian Sommer

item.title: Planetary biotechnospheres, biotechnosignatures and the search for extraterrestrial intelligence
item.description: arXiv:2611.33404v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The concept of planetary intelligence as collective intelligence is used to consider possible evolutionary paths of biotechnospheres that emerge on the intersection of the technosphere with the biosphere and support coupling of the technosphere with the biosphere, thus affecting planetary evolution. In mature biotechnospheres, the intelligence of technologies and the intelligence of life forms, including engineered life forms, could act in concert to perform various tasks (e.g. monitoring and restoring planetary environments and biodiversity; supporting space missions; terraforming cosmic objects). Space exploration can expand biotechnospheres beyond planets and create cosmic ecosystems. Humankind, other civilizations or their intelligent machines may produce biotechnosignatures (i.e. observables and artefacts of biotechnospheres) in the Solar System and beyond. I propose ten possible biotechnosignatures and strategies for the search for these biotechnosignatures in situ and over interstellar distances. For example, if a non-human advanced civilization existed and built biotechnospheres on Earth in the past, the descendants of its engineered bacteria could currently exist on Earth and have properties pertaining to the functions of the ancient bacteria in the biotechnospheres; intelligent technologies created by the ancient civilization could migrate to the Solar System's outer regions; these two scenarios are described as the Cosmic Descendants hypothesis. Interstellar asteroids, free-floating planets, spacecraft and objects gravitationally bound to flyby stars might carry extraterrestrial biotechnospheres and pass through the Solar System. In connection to the fate of post-main-sequence stars and their Oort clouds, the probability for interstellar asteroids to carry biotechnospheres or to be interstellar spacecraft is estimated as very low.
item.dc:creator: Irina K. Romanovskaya

item.title: Weak buoyancy and cold lithospheres decouple interior melting from seafloor volcanism on icy ocean worlds
item.description: arXiv:2611.33478v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: On icy ocean worlds, deep silicate melting can generate sufficient pressure to open fractures while magma freezes before reaching the ocean. We identify a coupled transport regime by linking finite melt segregation and nonlinear rock relaxation to fracture flow, crystallisation and the ice-loaded ocean boundary. In a hot Europa endmember, increasing grain size from 1 to 10 mm raises relaxed excess pressure from 5.55 kPa to 10.2 MPa, overcoming the inherited-fracture opening threshold despite weak buoyancy. For the same 100 m strike and 0.5 m aperture, the cold first-fill rate required by heat balance increases from 0.17-0.69 m3 s -1 over terrestrial crustal distances of 1.1-4.5 km to 15-29 m3 s -1 across 89-171 km Europa paths, far above the self-supplied flow. Higher ice-ocean pressure further reduces the enthalpy margin of near-solidus magma in the adopted basalt phase law. During approximately 5 kyr of dormancy, the collector pressure returns to its relaxed value, while upper-path walls cool to 275-282 K and the magma path loses liquid connectivity. In two focused Europa histories with mechanically supported pathways, delivery of 0.005 km3 of magma over 0.1 Myr requires 14-27 km3 of sacrificed magma-equivalent preparation material. Weak gravity, extensive cold rock and a pressurised ocean thus make seafloor access a history-dependent process governed by thermal connectivity and its renewal, decoupling recurrent volcanism from melt production at depth.
item.dc:creator: Nahiz Hestaphin

item.title: Stellar Obliquities of Cold Jupiter and Brown Dwarf Systems I: Spin-Orbit Misalignment Grows with Orbital Eccentricity
item.description: arXiv:2611.33506v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Stellar obliquity provides insights into the formation and dynamical evolution of planetary systems. Most obliquity measurements to date have focused on close-in transiting giant planets, whose orbits may have been altered by migration and tidal interactions. In contrast, the stellar obliquities of cold Jupiters, the most common class of giant planets, remain largely unexplored. Here, we measure the minimum stellar obliquity for 69 cold Jupiters and brown dwarfs (M_p > 0.3 M_J, a > 1 au), by comparing stellar inclinations derived from stellar rotation measurements with companion orbital inclinations constrained by radial velocities, relative astrometry and Hipparcos-Gaia absolute astrometry. We find that spin-orbit misalignments are common among cold Jupiters and brown dwarf companions, with 19/69 (28 +6/-5%) exhibiting significant misalignments. Furthermore, the stellar obliquities depends strongly on orbital eccentricity, whereby 0/17 (0 +8/-0%) companions with e_orb <= 0.15 are misaligned, compared to 19/52 (37 +7/-6%) with more eccentric orbits. This pattern reveals a connection between orbital eccentricity and stellar obliquity: companions on nearly circular orbits tend to be aligned with their host stars, whereas those on eccentric orbits exhibit a broader range of obliquities. This finding suggests that post-formation dynamical interactions, such as planet-planet scattering or secular chaos, may play an important role in exciting both orbital eccentricities and spin-orbit misalignments.
item.dc:creator: Lauren I. Biddle, Jingwen Zhang

item.title: Planetary Habitable Zones around Magnetized White Dwarfs
item.description: arXiv:2611.33711v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: White dwarfs are known to host remnant planetary material, indicating that rocky objects can survive post-main-sequence evolution and migrate into very close orbits. However, the decline of white dwarf luminosity makes it difficult for a planet to remain habitable for long when relying only on the white dwarf's irradiative heating. While several non-radiative energy sources have been proposed, the role of white dwarf magnetism in planetary energy budgets remains largely unexplored. We examine whether magnetic unipolar induction could provide sustained heating for close-in rocky planets. By coupling white dwarf cooling tracks with an orbit-dependent induction model, we evaluate the contribution of ohmic dissipation to planetary surface energy budgets and estimate the upper limit with efficient heat deposition. It is possible for the induction heating to supply a nearly steady surface energy flux for certain orbital distances and stellar spins, partially offsetting the decline in the white dwarf irradiation at late times. This leads to a persistent outer temperate region and, in some cases, a narrow inner zone that emerges after substantial cooling, identifying magnetic induction as a viable long-lived supplement to radiative heating.
item.dc:creator: Xueyuan Wang, Cong Yu, Bo Ma, Di-Chang Chen, Jianheng Guo

item.title: Mass Spectral Evidence for Iron Sulfate in Venus' Cloud Aerosol
item.description: arXiv:2611.33945v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Venus' cloud aerosols play pivotal roles in the thermal, chemical, and optical properties of the atmosphere. Here, we present mass spectral evidence that the cloud aerosols contain abundant iron sulfates. Data from the Pioneer Venus Large Probe Neutral Mass Spectrometer (LNMS) suggest that cloud aerosols inadvertently collected into the inlets at ~48-51 km and thermally decomposed below the clouds, releasing several compounds into the LNMS. At 23 km and below, multiple iron species (54Fe+, 56FeO+, 54FeO+, 56Fe2O+, and 56Fe2O2+) and other decomposition gases were detected. Quantitative treatment of these mass signals suggested the release of Fe2O3, SO2, O2, SO3, H2SO4, and H2O, consistent with the thermal decomposition of hydronium-bearing ferric sulfates. The resulting mole ratio for iron to sulfate (2.0 +/- 1.1) aligns with hydronium jarosite ((H3O)Fe3(SO4)2(OH)6), which likely formed within the inlets after aerosol capture, dehydration, and loss of sulfuric acid. Our thermochemical calculations support these assessments. Speciation of the ferric sulfates in the native aerosols remains unconstrained (e.g., solution and/or particle phases). Peak fits to the thermal release profiles yielded the abundances of the bulk iron (0.8 +/- 0.4 mg m-3) and aerosol-derived compounds, including hydronium jarosite (2.2 +/- 1.2 mg m-3, 30 +/- 17 wt%), water (3.7 +/- 0.4 mg m-3, 50 +/- 10 wt%), and sulfuric acid (1.5 +/- 0.2 mg m-3, 20 +/- 5 wt%). Surface sourcing of the cloud iron is likely minor. Instead, cosmic dust influx could deliver iron to the clouds in a geologically short time (2.4 +/- 1.5 Myr).
item.dc:creator: Rakesh Mogul, Mikhail Yu. Zolotov, Michael J. Way, Sanjay S. Limaye

item.title: Halley's Comet Over New Zealand In 1910: An Overview Of A Spectacular Apparition
item.description: arXiv:2611.33170v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Halley's Comet (1P/Halley) returns to the inner Solar System approximately every 76 years. In 1910, the comet put on a particularly wonderful display, whereby the comet attained an apparent magnitude of 1 or brighter, and had a tail of up to 120{\deg} in length. Many New Zealanders saw Comet 1P/Halley and submitted articles to newspapers across the land. Those articles were mostly from lay-people who reported their observations of this, the most famous of all comets. There were, however, numerous serious amateur and professional astronomers who made detailed observations and took world-class photographs of the comet. In this paper, we present the results of a thorough search through historical records and media publications in Aotearoa/New Zealand, to investigate how extensively Comet 1P/Halley was observed from this island nation. Where appropriate, we compare the observations described with international accounts, and find that those made from Aotearoa/New Zealand often echo what observers were witnessing around the world. We find that thousands of New Zealanders observed Comet 1P/Halley in 1910, and that the comet raised the interest in astronomy across the land resulting in the establishment of a number of astronomical societies that remain active to the current day.
item.arxiv:journal_reference: Journal of Astronomical History and Heritage, 29(3), 563-636 (2026)

item.title: OSIRIS-REx Lessons Learned Report: Insights from the Journey to Bennu and Back
item.description: arXiv:2611.33214v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: OSIRIS-REx, NASA's third New Frontiers mission, was the first U.S. mission to return a sample from an asteroid. Proposed in 2010 for an \$811 million lifecycle cost, the mission was completed for \$828 million, returned more than \$52 million of Headquarters reserves unused, and delivered at least 121.6 g of pristine material from near-Earth asteroid (101955) Bennu in September 2023, more than twice the Level-1 requirement. It did so despite a surface far more rugged than predicted, the discovery of particle ejection, sampling in a regolith much weaker than expected, operations during the COVID-19 pandemic, and an off-nominal parachute sequence on Earth return. This report sets out the lessons learned by the mission's leadership across six areas: leadership and governance; cost, schedule and risk management; systems engineering; mission operations; sample return, curation and analysis; and data archiving. Recurring themes are that a PI-led structure integrating science, engineering and project management gives the discipline to make fast, informed decisions; that reserves and schedule margin spent early to retire risk, such as funding Natural Feature Tracking as a backup navigation system, buy the flexibility to absorb discovery; that heritage hardware reduces risk only when its verification and engineering knowledge are preserved; and that contamination knowledge, sample science and data stewardship are mission-long responsibilities, not post-flight tasks. Each section pairs background with specific recommendations for future sample-return and small-body missions.
item.dc:creator: Dante S. Lauretta, Heather L. Enos, C. W. V. Wolner

item.title: line racer: Rapid Calculation of Exoplanetary Radiative Opacities
item.description: arXiv:2611.33290v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Detailed studies of exoplanet and brown dwarf atmospheres rely on precise knowledge of the spectral features of possible atmospheric species. These features are a result of the interaction of different molecules and atoms with the radiation of the host star or the intrinsic thermal radiation of the object. The interaction is described by the opacity of a species, which determines how much light is absorbed at a given wavelength. The strength and shape of these opacities are very dependent on the temperature and pressure of the atmosphere, which is why they have to be calculated for a wide range of conditions. line racer is a Python package that enables computing high-resolution opacities from large molecular and atomic line lists in an effective manner. It offers users a wide range of options to customize opacity calculations to their needs and available hardware. The code is designed for efficient parallelization on multi-core and multi-node systems and can produce outputs compatible with popular atmospheric modeling and retrieval tools.
item.dc:creator: David B. H\"agele, Paul Molli\`ere, Michiel Min

item.title: Moon Radio Interferometer for Science and Exploration (MoonRISE): A Mission Concept for a Low-Frequency Radio Interferometer on the Lunar Farside
item.description: arXiv:2611.33534v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The universe below 20 MHz remains one of space science's last unexplored frontiers, inaccessible from Earth due to its ionosphere and terrestrial radio frequency interference (RFI). We present the mission concept for the Moon Radio Interferometer for Science and Exploration (MoonRISE), an all-sky imaging, low-frequency radio telescope operating from 100 kHz-30 MHz from the lunar farside, the quietest radio environment in the inner Solar System. If realized, MoonRISE would be the first radio interferometer on the Moon and the first connected-element radio interferometer in space. Its science objectives are to (1) determine how solar wind turbulence drives plasma heating, acceleration, and space weather evolution in the inner heliosphere, by measuring the scattering of type III solar radio bursts between 2-20 solar radii; (2) constrain the density, structure, and variability of the lunar ionosphere and its effects on surface communication; and (3) resolve the plasma sources and magnetospheric dynamics that power Uranian Kilometric Radiation, observable for the first time since Voyager 2 in 1986. The same observations would yield all-sky maps of the low-frequency sky, subsurface structure at the landing site, and a characterization of the farside RF environment. The Radio Interferometer concept consists of nine 3.5 m dipoles embedded in a 1.5 km optical-fiber tether deployed by a rover, with power- and RF-over-fiber enabling RFI-free mapping. A rover-mounted Ground Penetrating Radar (300-2000 MHz) would measure regolith dielectric properties and bedrock depth to characterize the dipoles' RF performance. We describe the science objectives, a reference landing site in Lacus Luxuriae, a notional concept of operations, and the payload design and technology maturity. The concept builds on SunRISE and OVRO-LWA heritage and could serve as a basis for a future selected mission.

item.title: Formation of Electron Velocity Distribution Functions at low-\{beta} Quasi-Perpendicular Shocks From Physical-Mass-Ratio PIC Simulations
item.description: arXiv:2611.33989v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: At low-\{beta} quasi-perpendicular shocks, the origins of upstream field-aligned electron beams and downstream flat-top distributions remain unresolved. Using 2D fully kinetic particle-in-cell (PIC) simulations at the physical ion-to-electron mass ratio (mi/me = 1836), we found that the shock transition region is dominated by electromagnetic whistler-mode turbulence driven by the modified two-stream instability (MTSI) of reflected ions, not by the electrostatic instabilities as suggested by some previous studies using a reduced mass ratio. Beams in the upstream are produced mainly by shock-drift acceleration (SDA) at the ramp, whereas we attribute the downstream flat-top distributions to nonuniform acceleration by the parallel electric field. Electrons experience different field strengths, polarities, and interaction durations along their trajectories, leading to a spread of parallel velocity changes that broadens and flattens the distribution. These results highlight the importance of using the physical mass ratio in exploring the electron dynamics of low-\{beta} shocks.
item.dc:creator: Zhoufan Mu, Yao Chen, Hao Ning, Shan Wang, Sibo Xu, Terry Zixu Liu, Ao Guo, Hui Zhang, Hui Zhu

item.title: Flare driven habitability: Expanding life's potential around low-mass stars
item.description: arXiv:2603.24944v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The traditional definition of the circumstellar habitable zone (HZ) focuses on liquid water, but neglects the crucial role of ultraviolet (UV) radiation in prebiotic chemistry. Low-mass stars typically emit insufficient UV radiation for photochemistry throughout the liquid water HZs during quiescent states. However, frequent flares can provide substantial UV fluxes, potentially fostering habitable conditions. We refine the concept of a UV habitable zone (UV-HZ) by incorporating a temperature-dependent model for RNA precursor synthesis. Furthermore, we explore a parameterized spectral energy distribution model and adopt an empirical flare frequency distribution for flares on different stars to quantify their UV contribution. Applying this framework to different flaring stars, we find the UV-HZ around low-mass stars can extend to inner regions, and overlap with the traditional HZ in wide ranges. Apply the analysis to 9 planets around Kepler flaring stars, three planets are located within both the refined UV-HZ and liquid water habitable zone (LW-HZ) without causing ozone depletion. Our findings highlight the significant role of flares in expanding the potential for life around low-mass stars, offering a revised perspective on exoplanet habitability criteria.
item.dc:creator: Dong-Yang Gao, Hui-Gen Liu, Ming Yang, Ji-Lin Zhou

item.title: A comprehensive study of comet 67P/Churyumov-Gerasimenko in the 2021/2022 apparition. II. Colorimetry, polarimetry, modeling
item.description: arXiv:2607.20038v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: This paper presents the second part of our multi-technique observational study of comet 67P during its 2021-2022 apparition. While the first paper focused on photometry and spectroscopy, here we investigate the dust color and linear polarization of the coma. Imaging in the g-sdss and r-sdss filters was obtained with the 6-m BTA SAO Telescope, and aperture polarimetry was performed with the 2.6-m Shajn Telescope (CrAO) and the 2-m RCC Telescope. Observations at phase angles of 47.9 deg (6 October 2021) and 10.5 deg (6 February 2022) show negative polarization of about 0.5-2.5% at 10.5 deg and positive polarization of about 11% at 47.9 deg. The dust color was red, reaching about 0.8 mag near the nucleus and in the tail, and decreasing to about 0.2 mag in the coma and jet within 20,000 km of the nucleus. Spatial maps reveal a gradual decrease in color index and a corresponding increase in polarization with distance from the nucleus. Numerical modeling using ballistic particle-cluster aggregates composed of equal fractions of silicates and organics indicates that the coma is dominated by particles larger than 10 micrometers, while local polarization enhancements are consistent with regions containing smaller (1-10 micrometer) grains. Combining our aperture measurements with published data from four previous apparitions confirms that comet 67P belongs to the high-polarization class. The unusually high positive polarization observed during the 2021/22 apparition, together with the relatively isotropic coma morphology, suggests that the dust properties may have changed after the 2015/16 apparition.
item.dc:creator: Vera Rosenbush, Oleksandra Ivanova, Johannes Markkanen, Igor Lukyanyk, Valerii Kleshchonok, Ludmilla Kolokolova, Colin Snodgrass, Elena Shablovinskaya

item.title: Linking Outer Solar System Objects in Archival DECam Imaging: A Multi-year Linker Tested on Held-out Known Objects, and 273 Multi-opposition Candidates Including Six L4 Neptune Trojans, Two Retrograde Objects and Ten with a > 150 au
item.description: arXiv:2611.14330v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: I link single-night detections in public DECam imaging: 74% of the NOIRLab Source Catalog DR2 (2012-2019) sky with four or more nights, and my extraction from 149,421 exposures (2020-2026). Of 931 secure known objects, single-season linking recovers 22.1-25.0%, a multi-year linker 26.5%, together 36.2%. The multi-year rule, fixed before its held-out tests, recovers 68% of DES objects brighter than r=23.5 in a strip of its footprint and 14 of 47 known objects outside it. Its shifted-sky controls, complete for 162 of 165 blocks, return no candidate. This limits pure chance alignments, not links that mix real and chance detections. An identity check by orbit with 3,110 joint fits finds no designated object among the candidates. Searches beyond 79 au recover, blind, only 2014 UZ224, Gonggong and Chiminigagua. The catalogue has 273 undesignated candidates with orbits from two or more oppositions, whose linked detections were re-measured on the images; of the 189 of version 2, 41 were then detected on two or more nights that their fits did not use. Listed apart are 92 weaker entries and 30 designated objects, 17 of them Rubin discoveries with 2.9-13.2 yr of arc before discovery. Six are candidate L4 Neptune Trojans whose orbits and clones librate for 10 Myr (one reported independently by Jongma 2026, mostly from other data), two are retrograde candidates and ten have a>150 au. There is no follow-up or validated selection function. The Minor Planet Center has astrometry of 38 objects; unreleased positions are available on request, in confidence.
item.dc:creator: Gioele Cerati

item.title: Thermal evolution of Uranus and Neptune, hydrogen-water phase separation and the role of methane
item.description: arXiv:2611.32107v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Adiabatic evolution models of Uranus and Neptune with constant compositional stratification miss their observed luminosities: Uranus is fainter than commonly predicted, while improved equations of state (EoS) have recently led to a brightness problem for Neptune. In adiabatic models of Jupiter and Saturn, helium rain is thought to enhance luminosity. In the ice giants, hydrogen-water phase separation (H2-H2O demixing) with water rain has recently been predicted. We aim to understand how H2-H2O demixing and the EoS of water influence the luminosity of Uranus and Neptune. We use state-of-the-art EoS of H, He, H2O, and the H2-H2O phase diagram to build adiabatic three-layer models of the present-day structure that match the observed gravity field and the phase diagram. We compute evolution tracks with and without demixing, and for Neptune, with and without latent heat and methane, for which we provide an updated large-scale EoS including entropy. Without demixing, adiabatic Neptune with the revised AQUA EoS, without methane or latent heat, cools to its observed luminosity within 4.5 Gyr, in good agreement with the age of the Solar system. Applying the same assumptions to Uranus would require a Bond albedo of 0.43 to explain its luminosity. With demixing, the radii expand while the luminosity decreases. For Uranus, demixing leads to an equilibrium evolution with the incident flux that naturally explains its faintness. Demixing also makes Neptune fainter. Methane reduces the radius expansion but not the faintness problem. Favored Neptune models include demixing and methane at an initial C/O ratio of $\sim$1 due to CO ice accretion, with cooling times of $\lesssim 4 Gyr. Neptune requires an additional heat source unless its structure is primordial and the outer envelope is ice-poor, while hydrogen-water phase separation is an option to explain the structure and faintness of Uranus.
item.dc:creator: Marina Cano Amoros, Nicola Tosi, Nadine Nettelmann

item.title: Hyrax: An Extensible Framework for Rapid ML Experimentation and Unsupervised Discovery in the Era of Rubin, Roman, and Euclid
item.description: arXiv:2605.18959v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: The NSF-DOE Vera C. Rubin Observatory, Roman Space Telescope, Euclid, and other next-generation surveys will deliver imaging, spectroscopic, and time-domain data at scales that increasingly shift the bottleneck in astronomical machine learning (ML) projects from model design to infrastructure. We present Hyrax, an open-source, modular, GPU-enabled Python framework that supports the full ML lifecycle in astronomy: from data acquisition and training to inference and experiment comparison, with capabilities including multimodal dataset support, integrated vector databases for similarity search, and interactive two- and three-dimensional latent-space exploration for unsupervised discovery. We demonstrate Hyrax's versatility through five representative applications on real survey data: (i) unsupervised representation learning on $\sim 4\times10^5$ Rubin Legacy Survey of Space and Time (LSST) Data Preview 1 (DP1) galaxies, surfacing new merger and low-surface-brightness candidates missing from reference Euclid and Dark Energy Survey catalogs, while also isolating imaging artifacts -- all without labeled training data; (ii) hybrid density-based clustering for identifying cluster-scale gravitational lens candidates in DP1 data; (iii) multimodal early-time transient classification in the Zwicky Transient Facility leveraging light curves, spectra, images, and metadata; (iv) supervised false-positive filtering in shift-and-stack searches for distant solar system objects in the Dark Energy Camera Ecliptic Exploration Project survey; and (v) supervised detection of semi-resolved dwarf galaxies in Hyper Suprime-Cam and LSST-like imaging using synthetic source injection. Together, these results demonstrate that Hyrax provides astronomy-specific ML infrastructure that enables systematic discovery and rapid methodological iteration across next-generation astronomical surveys.
